content.content:
---
name: verify-in-production
description: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
---

# Verify in production

A change is finished when someone has watched it work. Most changes you can watch **now**, and
that is the rule — this skill is only for the rest: a change whose proof lives somewhere the
repo cannot see yet. You are filing the proof, not doing the work — and the proof itself runs
unattended: an automatic check, end to end, with a person entering
only where no automatic check can exist.

## When it fires: after the merge, never before

**The PR must have merged.** This skill runs as a step of the merge, unasked — `merge-to-main`
calls it once the squash has landed — and at no other moment. Not when the code is written, not
when the PR opens, not while review is in flight.

The reason is that a PR can be **rejected**, and a branch that is still open can be rewritten
under you. Both leave a verification whose premise never reached `main`:

- A **rewritten branch** makes the brief describe a change that no longer exists. #1121 was filed
  against a scope its PR then dropped; the verification was moot before the merge it waited on.
- A **rejected PR** is worse, because the queue cannot tell it from a merge. A blocked item
  releases on its blocker being *closed*, and nothing reads `merged` — so the item goes ready,
  reads an `In-production-when:` that can never become true, pushes `Not-before:` forward by
  `Retry-every:` without comment, and repeats indefinitely. No janitor rule reclaims it: the
  stale-ready sweep cannot see an item sleeping on a future `Not-before`, and the
  stuck-dependency sweep exempts an item whose blockers have closed.

So there is no such thing as filing this early and letting the queue sort it out. Wait for the
merge, then read **what actually landed** — the merged diff, not the branch you remember writing.

## First: does this file anything at all?

Most changes **file nothing.** Run the test in this order and stop at the first answer:

1. **Did you watch it work in this session?** Then it is proven. File nothing.
2. **Did a test that ran prove it?** A unit test, a CI job, an executable-requirements or UI
   test covering exactly the behaviour that changed. File nothing — the suite is the mechanism
   that comes back.
3. **Does the change have an observable effect at all?** A comment, a design doc, a README, a
   rename with no behavioural edge, a refactor a passing suite already pins. File nothing.
4. **Otherwise: where does its effect first become observable?** If the answer is a place and a
   moment — a member repo once it converges, a site once it deploys, a session once it reloads
   its rules — that is what you file.

The bar is *could not be watched now*, not *would be nice to double-check*. A verification
filed for a change already covered by a test is a wasted run re-proving what the suite proved.

## What you file

**A deferred request** — the same ad-hoc lane `/do-later` rides, so the queue does the waiting,
the running and the lifecycle; nothing here adds machinery beside it. One issue, titled
`Verify in production: <the change, in a few words>`, its body the whole brief: the run that
verifies will never see this conversation and may be days away. **Every field a run reads is one
block on the first lines of the description**, ahead of your prose — the same placement
[`/do-later`](../do-later/SKILL.md) files under, and what gives the retry below one place to
rewrite `Not-before:`. Then say what changed and why it could not be watched now.

```
Original-issue: #<the change's issue>
In-production-when: <the concrete artifact to read, and what makes it true>
Verify: <what to observe, and what counts as a pass>
Not-before: <ISO instant just past the expected release>
Retry-every: <how far to push Not-before when not yet live, e.g. 1 day>
Model: sonnet
```

No `Blocked-by:`. You are filing after the merge, so the change's PR has already closed and
there is nothing left to wait on but the release itself.

- **`Original-issue:`** is where a failure lands — the issue the change was done under, which
  the run reopens if the verification fails. Make the verification that issue's **sub-issue**
  too (`mcp__github__sub_issue_write`, method `add`, `issue_number` the original,
  `sub_issue_id` the **id** the create call returned, not its number), so the change it proves
  shows what is still unproven about it — [RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Filing an issue that
  belongs under another*, applied where there is no PR left to carry the link.
- **`In-production-when:`** names a thing to *read*, never a duration to wait. "`missingbulb/Shepherd`'s
  `.claudinite-settings.json` stamps `packVersions.tidy-repo` at 8 or higher." "The live site's
  `/version.json` reports a version past 4.2.0." "Any session started after this landed — check
  the vendored copy under `.claudinite/shared/` carries the new text." A merge is not a
  production condition, and neither is elapsed time.
- **`Verify:`** is an assertion with a pass condition, not a topic — and a read an **unattended
  run can make**: an API response, a file at a URL, an issue's state. "Issue #100 on that repo
  is closed with a comment citing the scheduler runs" beats "check tidy-issues works". Only where no
  automatic check can exist may `Verify:` name a person's step, spelled out exactly.
- **`Not-before:`** is the queue's own wait field: adoption holds the run until the moment has
  passed. Aim it just past the release you expect — the re-arm covers a miss, so don't pad it.
- **`Retry-every:`** is the extension you are prescribing: when the run finds the change not
  yet live, it re-arms `Not-before:` to **now + `Retry-every:`** — never the old value plus it.
  Size it to the release you wait on — a nightly converge retries daily, a next-session rule in
  minutes.

Then the mark, as `/do-later` applies it: **`task:origin:ad-hoc`**, the one label the scheduler
run adopts. `Model: sonnet` is in the block above because that is the work: reading a live
artifact and judging an assertion against it. Never `Automerge:` — a verification has nothing to
merge. If the mark doesn't exist in the repo yet, say so and leave the issue — it appears on the
next scheduler run.

## Tell the run how to converge

End the body with instructions to the run itself — the issue is its whole brief, and the run
decides nothing: it executes this playbook.

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real artifact. Never infer it from a merge, a green
   run, or elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the evidence actually read (the version, the value,
   the URL) and close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen `Original-issue:` with a comment
   saying what was asserted, what happened instead and where you read it; comment here linking
   that; close this issue as completed — the verification did its job by finding the fault.
3. **Not yet live** → set `Not-before:` to **now + `Retry-every:`** — the instant you are
   reading this at, never the old value the field carries — **clear the issue's
   `task:status:*` label** (clearing the status is the whole of the re-ask — the mark stays on
   for life), and leave the issue open. The next scheduler run re-adopts it, and the bumped
   field holds it until the new moment. No comment; the bumped field is the record.

   Measuring from the old value is what #1160 did: the queue releases a sleeping item on the
   first hourly pass past its instant, so by the time a run reads the field it is already
   behind — old + `Retry-every: 1 day` lands in the past again, the item goes ready on the very
   next pass, and a daily retry spends a session an hour.

## Then say what you filed

One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, and its retry cadence.

input.title: Verify in production: the executor's `toJSON(vars)` line does not get the workflow held for approval
input.body:
Original-issue: #1492
In-production-when: `missingbulb/Claudinite` has at least one `Claudinite executor` workflow run whose head sha is `e846728` or later (the squash of #1494, which put `CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}` into `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml`).
Verify: List those executor runs. PASS = every one of them created at least one job and none concluded `action_required`. FAIL = any run concluded `action_required`, or concluded in about a second having created zero jobs — that is GitHub's malicious-workflow hold, and it means `toJSON(vars)` is flagged the way `toJSON(secrets)` was in #1336.
Not-before: 2026-09-01T06:15:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day
Model: sonnet

## Why this could not be watched now

#1494 added one static line to the executor's work step:

```yaml
CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}
```

The reader is fully unit-tested against synthetic JSON, so nothing about *parsing* a bag needs production. What no test can reach is the claim the whole change rests on: **that serialising the `vars` context does not trip GitHub's [malicious-workflow detection](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-07-28-github-actions-holds-potentially-malicious-workflows-for-approval/)** the way serialising `secrets` did in #1336.

That claim is inference plus field evidence, not a guarantee:

- GitHub publishes no detection signals, thresholds or false-positive rate.
- `vars` is the context GitHub's own docs define as non-sensitive and render unmasked in build logs, so the exfiltration reading does not apply — but that is our reasoning, not GitHub's statement.
- `packs/static-website/stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml` and `static-site-deploy-pages.yml` have both passed `toJSON(vars)` since before the safeguard shipped without a park — strong evidence, from a different workflow than this one.

The failure mode is why this is worth a run rather than a shrug: a held run creates **zero jobs** and concludes `action_required` in about a second, which from the queue's side is indistinguishable from "nothing was pickable". #1336 ate executor runs in two repos for hours before anyone noticed, and #1330 mis-diagnosed it as a repository setting. Nothing red appears. Only reading run conclusions finds it.

The canon's scheduler is on `44 5,17 * * *`, so its drain dispatches the executor twice a day; `Not-before:` is aimed just past the first tick after the merge.

## Instructions to the run

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the Actions API — the real run list, never a merge, a green CI job or elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`.
   - Passes: comment the run ids and conclusions you actually read, and close this issue as completed.
   - Fails: reopen #1492 with a comment naming the held run, its conclusion and its job count, and say that `toJSON(vars)` must come out of `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml` and `packs/claudinite-tasks/stubs/claudinite-executor.yml` — the fleet is exposed to a silent park until it does. Comment here linking that, then close this issue as completed.
3. **Not yet live** (no executor run at or past that sha) → set `Not-before:` to the instant you are reading this at plus `Retry-every:`, clear this issue's `task:status:*` label, and leave it open. No comment.

{"id":5298546257,"number":1492,"state":"closed","state_reason":"completed","locked":false,"title":"The executor carries repo variables as one `toJSON(vars)` bag","body":"A task that needs a repository **variable** today pays what a task needing a **secret** pays: the executor workflow must name it statically, `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot write, so a new value needs a human-merged PR in every member — the coupling that wedged one in #1296.

For secrets that cost was taken back deliberately in #1336/#1337, because the one-line alternative, `toJSON(secrets)`, is the shape GitHub's [malicious-workflow detection](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-07-28-github-actions-holds-potentially-malicious-workflows-for-approval/) flags: every run parks with zero jobs until a person clicks Approve, silently.

**That reasoning does not carry to `vars`.**

- The safeguard's stated threat model is credential theft. `vars` is the context GitHub's own docs define as non-sensitive — *"Variables provide a way to store and reuse non-sensitive configuration information […] By default, variables render unmasked in your build outputs. If you need greater security for sensitive information, such as passwords, use secrets instead."* Dumping a context GitHub already renders unmasked in logs is not an exfiltration signal.
- `${{ toJSON(vars) }}` is a mainstream pattern with Marketplace actions built to consume it. Flagging it would be a mass false-positive event.
- **We already field it.** `packs/static-website/stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml:62` and `static-site-deploy-pages.yml:70` both pass `REPO_VARS_JSON: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}`, and have since before the safeguard shipped. No park. `read-config.mjs:41` already states the reasoning: *"`toJSON(vars)`, a context that structurally cannot carry a secret."*

## The change

One static line in the executor's work step, never regenerated, never a function of the task set:

```yaml
CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}
```

- A reader beside `secrets-bag.mjs`, sharing its bag mechanics rather than copying them, with the same fall-back-to-plain-env posture that makes the pre-PR window uneventful.
- `taskEnv` unpacks it, so a task's code-work reads `process.env.<NAME>` for any repo variable with nothing naming it in YAML. Unlike the secrets bag there is no per-task selection: vars are non-sensitive by construction, so the blast-radius argument that justified `required_secrets` has nothing to bite on.
- The scheduler stub is untouched. It runs no task code, and its one named variable is the operator hold, which every entry point must read before any bag exists.
- The `toJSON(secrets)` guard stays exactly as strict, and gains a sibling asserting the vars line IS present.

## Caveat carried in the code, not just here

GitHub publishes no detection signals, thresholds or false-positive rate. This is inference from the threat model, the docs and our own field evidence — not a guarantee. If it ever did fire, the failure mode is the silent `action_required` park that cost a mis-diagnosis in #1330.

{"id":5298546257,"number":1492,"state":"closed","state_reason":"completed","locked":false,"title":"The executor carries repo variables as one `toJSON(vars)` bag","body":"A task that needs a repository **variable** today pays what a task needing a **secret** pays: the executor workflow must name it statically, `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot write, so a new value needs a human-merged PR in every member — the coupling that wedged one in #1296.

For secrets that cost was taken back deliberately in #1336/#1337, because the one-line alternative, `toJSON(secrets)`, is the shape GitHub's [malicious-workflow detection](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-07-28-github-actions-holds-potentially-malicious-workflows-for-approval/) flags: every run parks with zero jobs until a person clicks Approve, silently.

**That reasoning does not carry to `vars`.**

- The safeguard's stated threat model is credential theft. `vars` is the context GitHub's own docs define as non-sensitive — *"Variables provide a way to store and reuse non-sensitive configuration information […] By default, variables render unmasked in your build outputs. If you need greater security for sensitive information, such as passwords, use secrets instead."* Dumping a context GitHub already renders unmasked in logs is not an exfiltration signal.
- `${{ toJSON(vars) }}` is a mainstream pattern with Marketplace actions built to consume it. Flagging it would be a mass false-positive event.
- **We already field it.** `packs/static-website/stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml:62` and `static-site-deploy-pages.yml:70` both pass `REPO_VARS_JSON: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}`, and have since before the safeguard shipped. No park. `read-config.mjs:41` already states the reasoning: *"`toJSON(vars)`, a context that structurally cannot carry a secret."*

## The change

One static line in the executor's work step, never regenerated, never a function of the task set:

```yaml
CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}
```

- A reader beside `secrets-bag.mjs`, sharing its bag mechanics rather than copying them, with the same fall-back-to-plain-env posture that makes the pre-PR window uneventful.
- `taskEnv` unpacks it, so a task's code-work reads `process.env.<NAME>` for any repo variable with nothing naming it in YAML. Unlike the secrets bag there is no per-task selection: vars are non-sensitive by construction, so the blast-radius argument that justified `required_secrets` has nothing to bite on.
- The scheduler stub is untouched. It runs no task code, and its one named variable is the operator hold, which every entry point must read before any bag exists.
- The `toJSON(secrets)` guard stays exactly as strict, and gains a sibling asserting the vars line IS present.

## Caveat carried in the code, not just here

GitHub publishes no detection signals, thresholds or false-positive rate. This is inference from the threat model, the docs and our own field evidence — not a guarantee. If it ever did fire, the failure mode is the silent `action_required` park that cost a mis-diagnosis in #1330.

{"clone_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/shepherd","message":"Repo `missingbulb/shepherd` added. Clone it NOW — ONE clone, inline in this turn, not a subagent and not in parallel with anything else (the session's git proxy caps this repo at 2 concurrent smart-HTTP ops; a second clone 429s both). Run `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/missingbulb/shepherd /home/user/shepherd` — and give it a GENEROUS command timeout (≈10 min), not the default. A large repo's shallow pack can take 5–10 minutes through the proxy; the default ~2-min timeout will kill `git index-pack` mid-unpack and leave a broken half-clone. `index-pack` looks stalled while unpacking a big pack but isn't — do NOT interrupt, kill, or re-run it just because it's still going. 

If /home/user/shepherd already exists when you go to clone: do NOT `rm -rf` it reflexively — it may be a live clone (yours, or another turn's; this 'added' result is exactly what a second concurrent add sees). Check: `git -C /home/user/shepherd rev-parse HEAD` — if it succeeds, it's done, just use it. If it fails, watch `du -sh /home/user/shepherd/.git` across a few checks ~15s apart: if it's growing, a clone is live — wait. Only if rev-parse still fails AND `.git` has been the same size for ~60s is the clone dead. Even then, check `ls -A /home/user/shepherd` first: if it lists anything other than `.git`, the directory is NOT a dead half-clone — STOP, do not delete it, and tell the user the path is occupied. Only if it contains nothing but `.git`: `rm -rf /home/user/shepherd` then run the clone command above exactly once. 

If the clone fails with HTTP 429 / "Too many concurrent git operations", that is this session's local concurrency cap — NOT a GitHub rate limit. Sleep 10s (the Retry-After value) then retry exactly once. Do NOT retry in a loop and do NOT spawn more workers to try a different way. 

(Shallow. Need more history for blame/log/bisect? Prefer a bounded `git -C /home/user/shepherd fetch --depth=1000 origin BRANCH` — some repos' git policy hooks block `--unshallow`/`--deepen`, and a bounded fetch works either way. Before pushing a branch from this clone, run `git -C /home/user/shepherd fetch origin DEFAULT_BRANCH` (then rebase if needed) so the push sends a thin pack — pushing from a stale shallow clone re-uploads the whole tree and the request is rejected with HTTP 413.) After the clone succeeds, briefly report the outcome to the user and ask what they want to do with it. Do NOT say 'ready to clone' — the user already approved. Session currently has 2 repo(s): missingbulb/claudinite, missingbulb/shepherd.

I dropped the `FOLLOW_MINUTES=30` I'd first drafted: `code_work_timeout` is 1800s and the 20-minute default is what that budget is sized around, so 30 would have eaten the margin the final report needs. Members will hold `vars-bag.mjs` with no bag to read — the harmless near-side window the `stamping-executor` fixture covers, but the capability doesn't reach them until a per-member workflow PR lands. > ⚠️ Still open: > • Baseline run in flight — waiting 10 min, then I'll report per member from the stamps. > • The `CLAUDINITE_VARS` line needs a per-member PR to reach the fleet; the baseline can't carry it. content.text:
You're right to push, and my "13 human PRs" answer was wrong. I'd been repeating the corpus line as if it were a platform law. It isn't — here's what the code actually says.

**The lane you're describing exists.** `engine/migrations/registry.mjs:87-121` has a dedicated path for materializing into `.github/workflows/`, gated on an env handshake, `CLAUDINITE_CAN_WITHHOLD_WORKFLOWS=1`, by which a caller announces it can withhold those paths from its own commit and hand them to the apply stage. `packs/claudinite-canary-repo/migrations/2026-08-14-workflow-probe-current/` is documented as *"the first record to materialize into `.github/workflows/` (#649)"*. So this was built, and it worked.

**It was then deliberately retired in #1317.** In `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/pack-update.mjs:238`:

> *"A path under `.github/workflows/` is REFUSED, not diverted. […] Nothing needs to: a member's workflows are static after adoption (#1317)."*

That flow passes `env: {}`, so the handshake is never announced; its `write` hard-refuses any workflow path; and it actively sweeps away the staging directory the old lane used, *"the sweep is also how a member confirms the lane is gone."*

So: not impossible, and not a platform limit. A capability that was removed on a stated premise — **and my change is the first thing to falsify that premise.** Workflows are no longer static after adoption. That's the real finding here, and it's a better framing than anything in my last three messages.

Two things I turned up on the way that matter for whichever route you pick:

**A real bug.** `applyMaterializations` correctly reports `SKIPPED <dest> (workflow file; this caller cannot deliver one)`. `applyRewrites` has no such guard — it does `await write(file, next); done.push(file)`, and since the update flow's `write` silently drops workflow paths, **a migration that rewrites a workflow file reports success having written nothing.** Same surface, one side guarded. That would bite whoever tries this next.

**A trap.** `materialize` copies the template verbatim, which would overwrite each member's stamped `# claudinite:secrets` names — the converge writes those per member. So the record has to `rewrite` (insert the line, preserve the rest), not `materialize`. Which runs straight into the bug above.

Also worth knowing: `convergeWorkflows` is called only from `bootstrap.mjs`, never from the nightly. And `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`'s documented grant (`fleet-token.mjs`) is Metadata / Contents / Issues / Actions — no `Workflows` permission, which a fine-grained PAT would need to push a workflow change.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

Claudinite loaded, 9 packs, 38 checks, 14,000 rule tokens, 22 available skills, 550 personal preference tokens.

You were right, and my "13 human PRs" answer was wrong. Before building, let me state what I found, because it changes the framing.

**`.github/workflows/` was never impossible — the lane that delivered it was deliberately closed.**

`engine/migrations/registry.mjs:100` still carries the whole mechanism: a `CLAUDINITE_CAN_WITHHOLD_WORKFLOWS` env handshake, a `WORKFLOW_DEST` guard, and a skip-with-note for callers that can't deliver. `packs/claudinite-canary-repo/migrations/2026-08-14-workflow-probe-current/` is documented as *"the first record to materialize into `.github/workflows/` (#649)"*. So it worked, and it shipped.

Then #1317 closed it. `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/pack-update.mjs:238` now passes `env: {}` — so the handshake is permanently false — and its `write` hard-refuses workflow paths, on this stated premise:

> *Nothing needs to: a member's workflows are static after adoption (#1317).*

**That premise is exactly what my change falsifies.** The machinery is intact and dormant; what's missing is a capable caller.

So my earlier claim was right about today's engine but wrong about why — I quoted a rule as a platform fact when it's a reversed design decision, and I didn't follow the `#649 withhold-and-hand-to-the-agent` pointer sitting in the file I'd already read.

**One real bug found on the way.** `applyMaterializations` guards workflow dests and reports `SKIPPED`. `applyRewrites` (registry.mjs:140-155) has no such guard — it calls `write`, then unconditionally `done.push(file)`. Since the update flow's `write` silently drops workflow paths, **a rewrite record targeting a workflow file reports success while writing nothing.** That's a false green, and it's precisely the record shape this change needs.

Let me confirm the scope of what re-opening costs before I write anything.

input.body:
#1494 put `CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}` into the executor stub. Every member holds the reader as of `claudinite-tasks` 60831.3, and **not one holds the line** — because nothing delivers `.github/workflows/` any more.

## The premise that closed the lane is now false

The withhold-and-hand-to-the-agent path shipped in #649 and worked. `packs/claudinite-canary-repo/migrations/2026-08-14-workflow-probe-current/` is documented as *"the first record to materialize into `.github/workflows/`"*.

#1317 closed it on one stated ground, at `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/pack-update.mjs:238`:

> Nothing needs to: a member's workflows are static after adoption (#1317).

That was true when it was written. #1494 is the counterexample: a workflow change every member needs, with no route to them. The alternative on the table was 13 hand-opened PRs — which the canon's own standing decision rejects, because per-repo manual work reliably does not happen.

## What is actually still there

The lane was **emptied, not removed** — the `updates/*` convention, and exactly the reason it exists. All four seams survive:

| Seam | State |
|---|---|
| `registry.mjs` `WITHHOLD_CAPABLE_ENV` / `WORKFLOW_DEST` / skip-with-note | intact, live |
| `pack-update.mjs` `PENDING_DIR`, `stagedAt()` | emptied, addressable |
| `stagedFiles()` | live — the sweep uses it |
| `applyStageFor(specs, withheld)` | still takes and renders `withheld` |

What #1317 removed is four lines: `write` drops workflow paths (`:239`), `env: {}` makes the handshake permanently false (`:242`), the sweep deletes anything staged (`:266`), and `withheld` is hardcoded `[]` (`:311`).

**The credential question is settled.** The Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` can never push under `.github/workflows/` — that part of the doctrine is real, and GitHub rejects the whole ref, so writing one into a tree about to be pushed fails the entire converge. But the apply stage does not run on that token: it raises a work item for an agent session, and the Claude GitHub App carries `workflows: write`. That is what closes the loop, and it is why staging + apply-stage is the shape rather than a direct write.

## A false green found on the way

`applyMaterializations` guards workflow dests and reports `SKIPPED …(workflow file; this caller cannot deliver one)`. `applyRewrites` (`registry.mjs:140-155`) has no such guard:

```js
if (next !== text) { await write(file, next); done.push(file); }
```

`write` silently drops workflow paths, but `done.push(file)` runs regardless — so **a rewrite record targeting a workflow file reports success while writing nothing.** Nothing has hit it because no record rewrites a workflow yet; this change makes that the exact shape needed, so it must be fixed here. Two structurally-identical surfaces, one guarded.

## The work

1. `applyRewrites` gets the same guard and the same skip-with-note as `applyMaterializations`.
2. `pack-update.mjs` refills the four seams: stage workflow paths under `PENDING_DIR`, announce the handshake, collect the real `withheld`, and scope the sweep so it clears pre-existing staged files without deleting what this run just staged.
3. A `claudinite-tasks` migration record rewriting the executor to insert the `CLAUDINITE_VARS` line — a **rewrite**, not a materialize, so each member's own stamped `# claudinite:secrets` names survive. It carries `applyStage` so a session delivers the staged file.
4. Forced fleet delivery afterwards, since this is an engine-flow change.

Refs #1492, #1494, #1317, #649

content.text:
Found a real ordering hazard before shipping it. `packRecordsInGap` selects a record only while `recordVersion > installedVersion`, and the executing worker is the member's *own vendored* one — the vendor step replaces it on disk while the old code is still running. So on the cycle a member takes the new lifecycle pack, the record would run against the **old** dropping `write`, no-op, and then be stamped past and never selected again.

`minEngineVersion` gates on the engine only; it cannot express "needs lifecycle ≥ X". So the record must land *after* the lane has converged, not beside it.

content.text:
You were right to push back, and the answer was better than either of us framed it.

**A migration can do this. The lane existed, worked, and was deliberately closed** — not a platform limit. #649 shipped withhold-and-hand-to-the-agent; #1317 closed it on one premise, at `pack-update.mjs:238`: *"a member's workflows are static after adoption."* #1494 is the counterexample. My "13 human PRs" answer took a rule about the nightly push and inflated it into "impossible", and I'd read the `#649 withhold-and-hand-to-the-agent` pointer in that very file without following it.

The lane was *emptied, not removed*. All four seams survived, so [#1511](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1511) refills them rather than rebuilding anything.

**The credential detail that makes it work:** `GITHUB_TOKEN` genuinely can never push under `.github/workflows/` — GitHub rejects the whole ref, so a workflow file in the committed tree fails the *entire* update. That's why it's staging rather than a direct write. The apply stage runs on a different credential: the Claude GitHub App carries `workflows: write`.

**A live bug found on the way.** `applyRewrites` never had the workflow guard `applyMaterializations` has. Its caller's `write` dropped workflow paths silently while `done.push(file)` ran anyway — so a run that delivered no workflow reported it had. `chrome-release-vendoring` rewrites a workflow file and has been hitting this; its test passed the capable env to the materializations but not the rewrite. Same blind spot, fixed.

**Two things I pulled out rather than ship:**

`ENGINE_VERSION` is not bumped — `engine/version.mjs` says it advances by release after the canary rehearsal, never by an ordinary change. I'd nearly bumped it.

More importantly, **the record carrying the executor line isn't in this PR.** I built it, then found the ordering hazard: a record is selected only while its version exceeds the member's installed one, and the executing worker is the member's *own vendored* copy — the vendor step replaces it on disk while the old code still runs. Shipped beside the lane, the record would run against the old dropping `write`, no-op, get stamped past, and never be selected again. `minEngineVersion` gates the engine only and can't express "needs lifecycle ≥ X". The record is written and parked; it follows once the fleet carries the lane.

> ⚠️ Still open:
> • [#1511](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1511) awaits your review — not merged.
> • The executor record is parked in scratch, not committed. It lands as a follow-up gated on members stamping `claudinite-lifecycle` ≥ 60831.1; I'll file that issue on merge, not before, since an unmerged branch can be rewritten under it.
> • The `applyRewrites` guard ships to members only on the next **engine release**, not this pack cycle — the two lanes deliver separately.
> • [#1496](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1496) still waits on the canon's next executor run to prove `toJSON(vars)` isn't held for approval.
> • The 47-PR fleet backlog is untouched — that was a misread on my part and I've left it alone.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
